note.text: Volcanicity includes movement and emplacement of molten material in or onto Earth's crust. Magma remains below the surface; lava is magma erupted onto the surface. Intrusive features form below ground. A dyke cuts across existing layers; a sill lies along them. Extrusive features include lava flows and volcanic cones. Eruptions can also release ash and gases. Not all volcanic hazards are slow lava flows, and not every intrusion reaches the surface.

sections.heading: Apply the ideas locally
sections.text: Near Mount Cameroon, volcanic landforms can be discussed through maps and teacher-selected observations. This lesson is classroom preparation, not an invitation to approach an active vent. A section drawing distinguishes a sheet cutting layers from one following them. Classification depends on their relationship to the rock layers rather than only on the page's up/down direction.

sections.heading: Reason and check
sections.text: Ask whether the molten material stayed below ground or erupted. For a sheet intrusion, inspect whether it cuts across or follows the existing layers. Use correct terms for ash and gases, and keep physical landforms separate from the human effects of an eruption.
